title: the lac house
hook: the city mourns the living, and in the forest Bhima keeps watch

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house fell behind them: Bhima carrying everyone, and a boatman who knew Vidura's words — quiet help, hidden in plain sight. Did you help someone quietly? Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

In Hastinapura, the news arrives: the Pandavas are dead, burned at Varanavata with their mother. Dhritarashtra weeps, the text says, and orders the rites for the dead. Water is offered for them. The people mourn. And Vidura grieves only a little, because he knows. Far away, the five brothers and their mother are alive, and asleep on the ground. Today, the last of the lac house: two nights, and two kinds of grief.

In the forest, they've gone as far as they can. Kunti is exhausted and thirsty. Bhima goes to find water, and by the time he brings it back, they're all asleep, on the bare ground under a tree. So Bhima sits up, alone, and looks at them. The text gives him a lament here. In paraphrase: what could hurt more than this, my brothers sleeping on the earth, my mother lying in the open like this. He thinks of Duryodhana, and his anger rises. He could go back and end it, he says. But Yudhishthira isn't angry, and Bhima won't move without him. So he stays where he is, and keeps watch. Set the two scenes side by side. In the city, a king weeps for nephews his own son tried to kill. The text doesn't tell us how to weigh those tears. Vidura holds his secret and says little. And in the forest, the brother known for his strength, and for his anger, spends it sitting still. Bhima is the brother we first met shaking boys out of a tree. Here, at the end of the lac house, his strength takes another shape. He doesn't go back to fight. He stays awake so the others can rest. The house is ash. The family is homeless, mourned as dead, sleeping in the open. And one of them is watching over the rest.
screen: `ASLEEP ON THE BARE GROUND.` · `BHIMA'S LAMENT, AND HIS ANGER.` · `HE WON'T MOVE WITHOUT YUDHISHTHIRA.` · then, large: `STRENGTH THAT KEEPS WATCH.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow. Bring to mind the people who'll be asleep tonight, under your roof, or in your city, or far away: people you care about. If you live alone, think of one person, wherever they are. See them resting. For a moment, you're the one awake, like Bhima under the tree. There's nothing you need to do for them. Just keep watch in your mind, breathing slowly, while they sleep. The bell holds the time.
Bhima, the brother known for strength and anger, who spends this night sitting still, keeping watch while his family sleeps.
Your line: strength that keeps watch. Today, if anger rises, see whether it can turn into watchfulness instead, just once. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Offering water for the dead, called tarpana, is part of Hindu funeral and remembrance rites; in this story the offering is made for the Pandavas while they are still alive.

match.prompt: two nights of grief — tap the pairs.
pairs: grieves only a little; he knows

myth: the city knew the Pandavas were alive
the people mourned them as dead; Vidura knew.
Bhima went back that night to fight Duryodhana
he stayed and kept watch, because Yudhishthira wasn't angry.
the family slept on the bare ground
under a tree, while Bhima sat up and watched.

fork.setup: you're Bhima. your family is asleep on the ground, and the man who tried to burn them is in a palace. what do you do?
options: go back tonight and settle it.
wake Yudhishthira and argue for revenge.
stay where you are, and keep watch.
fork.reveal: he stays. his anger is real, the text says, but Yudhishthira isn't angry, so Bhima keeps watch while the others sleep.

original.note: Sanskrit bhīma: terrible, formidable; the name of the brother known for strength, who here uses his strength to sit still.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bhima is all muscle and temper.
what it means: at the lac house's end, his strength sits still and guards his sleeping family.
what a scholar hears: the text gives him a lament over his family on the bare ground, and has him hold back because Yudhishthira isn't angry.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha Parva (the mourning at Hastinapura; Dhritarashtra's grief and the water rites; Vidura grieves little)
Mahabharata, Adi Parva, opening of Hidimba-vadha Parva (Bhima fetches water and keeps watch; his lament over his sleeping family)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Dhritarashtra weeps and orders the funeral and water rites; Vidura grieves little because he knows.
Bhima's lament and his line that he would act but for Yudhishthira's lack of anger are paraphrased from the opening of the Hidimba-vadha section; confirm wording and placement.

Hidimba, Ghatotkacha, Ekachakra and Baka fall between this day and the swayamvara in the text; the outline passes over them, so this script ends the lac house before Hidimba arrives. A Keeper may want them named in passing.
The readings of Dhritarashtra's tears were cut in the editor pass (see below).

Editor pass: cut the 'some readers... some... both' reading of Dhritarashtra's tears (the device recurs on nearly every nearby day) and the unsourced superlatives 'most strength', 'most anger' and 'strongest brother'.
Audit pass: 'the one this poem usually shows breaking things' was an unsourced generalization; replaced with a callback to day 727's tree.
